storm.summary_layperson: No storm risk this evening — skies are clear and dry across the region, so the cove gets the same quiet, cooling evening as every surrounding town.
storm.local_effect_blurb: The weak cool layer over the 65°F Sound (6°F air–water gap at 4 PM) fades by about 4:50 PM as the air cools and is gone by sunset — no storms around for it to matter.
storm.detail_html:
Regional picture: a dry, sunny, breezy autumn afternoon behind a departed front. Radar is clear in every direction, there are no National Weather Service alerts, and the air is very dry (dew points in the low-to-mid 40s against 73°F air). The atmosphere has essentially zero storm fuel (CAPE 0 J/kg), and the model keeps it at zero through the evening.

Winds aloft are strong — about 60 kt of wind shear between the surface and 6 km — which on a humid day would be a warning sign for organized storms. With no instability and no moisture to work with, it is irrelevant tonight: there is nothing for that shear to organize.

Local effects: the Sound is 65°F and the air is about 72°F, a 6–7°F gap that leaves a weak layer of cooler, stable air over the water. That layer does not last. The Sound holds its temperature while the air cools toward and after sunset (6:24 PM), so the gap closes: it drops below the ~5°F level where it matters at about 4:50 PM, is essentially gone by 6 PM, and by 7 PM the air is forecast to be roughly 4°F colder than the water. There is also no sea breeze today — the wind is blowing offshore from the west-northwest. Neither local mechanism is helping or hurting, because there is nothing approaching to act on.

Most likely outcome: a dry, clear evening at the cove and in every surrounding town alike, cooling quickly from the low 70s into the low 60s after sunset. The only weather of note is the gusty offshore breeze, which eases after dark.

What would change the call: showers appearing on radar to the west or northwest, or a new advisory. Nothing in the current data points that way for this evening.

wind.regime_label: Moderate gradient wind — no sea breeze in play

hourly.shift_note: light after sunset, puffs further apart

wind.tactics_blurb: Gusty offshore west-northwesterly, about 11 kt gusting 18 at 5 PM and easing to 5 kt after the 6:24 PM sunset. Stay in the middle of the cove away from the shoreline holes and tack on the big 15–30° shifts — the best breeze is early.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
The call: moderate gradient wind — no sea breeze in play. The land is only about 6.5°F warmer than the Sound (71.6°F inland air against 65°F water), which is barely enough to drive a sea breeze on its own, and the background wind is blowing offshore at around 10 kt at the airports. Only 15% of coastal stations show any southerly flow. What you are sailing in is the large-scale west-northwesterly, not a thermal.

Right now at Riverside YC: NW 312° at 13 kt, gusting 20, with a 10-minute average of 13.5 kt. The mid-Sound buoy had WNW 17 gusting 23 on its last report (about 75 minutes old), so there is noticeably more breeze out in open water than inside the cove.

Model versus stations: the HRRR model has the wind due west (273°), but western-Sound stations sit at WNW (293°) and the yacht club itself reads NW (312°); the National Weather Service forecast also says northwest. The directions in the table take the model's hour-to-hour trend and shift it 20° to the right to match what the stations show. Expect the cove itself to read a further 10–15° right of the table in the puffs.

Through the window: because this is a gradient wind rather than a sea breeze, there is no sunset shut-off and the direction should hold all evening. The speed will not. The model drops from about 10 kt at 5 PM to 6 kt at 6 PM and 5 kt at 7 PM as the land cools quickly after the 6:24 PM sunset (air temperature falls roughly 10°F between 4 and 7 PM) and the breeze aloft stops mixing down to the surface in the lee of the shore. The 8–10 PM numbers are an extrapolation of that trend, not model output.

Where the pressure is: a west-northwest to northwest wind comes off the land, so it arrives in puffs and holes with swings of 15–30°. The best average pressure is usually in the middle of the cove, away from the immediate lee of the trees and houses on the western shore, with stronger and steadier breeze toward the mouth and out in the Sound. Play the oscillations rather than committing to a side.

What it feels like: 11 kt gusting 18 at 5 PM is powered-up, hiking conditions with real gains and losses on each shift. By 6 PM it is a pleasant 6–8 kt, and after 7 PM it is light air at 4–5 kt with the puffs getting further apart. The early part of the window is the good part.

data_caveats: HRRR model data only reached 7 PM this run (forecast hours beyond f04 were not yet available) — the 8–10 PM wind rows are extrapolated from the model's cooling trend, so treat them as lower confidence.
Model and stations differ on direction: HRRR has W 273°, western-Sound stations are WNW 293° and Riverside YC reads NW 312° — the table shifts the model 20° right to match the stations.
Gust figures are estimated from the current Riverside YC gust-to-average ratio; the model data carries no gust field.
Mid-Sound buoy 44040 reading is about 75 minutes old.
Westchester airport (KHPN) wind sensor is down; its temperature is still used.
Marine-layer trend only extends to 7 PM (same model gap).
